title: November 2026 Top500 New Systems Are Few and Far Between
gist: ServeTheHome's analysis of the November 2026 TOP500 finds only 28 new systems (lowest since tracking began in June 2018), ~5% total Rmax growth, and an average system age of ~3.2 years, as China and commercial Industry submissions have collapsed. Among new entries, Blackwell dominates accelerators, AMD leads CPUs with NVIDIA Grace tying Intel, and InfiniBand keeps taking share from Ethernet, while the author argues the list no longer reflects real HPC/AI investment.

insights.claim: The November 2026 TOP500 list has only 28 new systems by ServeTheHome's count (the official post says 27), the lowest since its tracking began in June 2018, down from 43 in June 2026 and versus 133 in June 2018 and 153 in November 2018.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The public TOP500 is a weakening proxy for HPC/AI hardware demand; do not read low turnover as low spending.
insights.quote: The November 2026 TOP500 list has only 28 new systems, the lowest count in our tracking series going back to June 2018.
insights.locator: New System Counts Hit a Series Low

insights.claim: The 28 new TOP500 systems contribute about 1.0 EF/s of Rmax, roughly 5.1% of total list performance, the lowest new-system share since at least November 2021 when new systems contributed over 12%.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Few large new systems are being publicly benchmarked with HPL.
insights.locator: The 28 new systems together contribute

insights.claim: Total TOP500 Rmax grew only about 5%, from roughly 18.7 EF/s in June 2026 to about 19.7 EF/s in November 2026, versus nearly 25% growth on the prior list driven largely by LineShine's debut.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Aggregate public supercomputer performance growth has stalled this cycle.
insights.locator: With so few new systems and modest newcomer performance

insights.claim: The TOP500 #500 entry threshold rose about 8% to roughly 2.87 PF/s, and only about 74% since November 2021's 1.65 PF/s, even though CPU performance has risen more than 4x as state-of-the-art went from 64-core AMD EPYC 7003 Milan to 256-core AMD EPYC 9006 Venice.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The entry bar lagging hardware gains confirms the list is not being refreshed with modern systems.
insights.locator: The #500 entry point rose

insights.claim: The average TOP500 system has now been on the list about 3.2 years, the highest in ServeTheHome's tracking window (up from about 2.2 years in November 2021), and the 28 systems that dropped off had averaged about 5.4 years on the list.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Aging installed base signals that list submissions, not deployments, are slowing.
insights.locator: The List Is Aging Rapidly

insights.claim: Of the 28 systems that dropped off the TOP500, 24 were CPU-only (mostly Intel Skylake or Cascade Lake from 2017-2019), 17 were Industry-segment, 17 were Lenovo-built and 14 were in China, while 23 of the 28 new systems are accelerated.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The list is rotating from old CPU-only commercial clusters to GPU-accelerated research systems, a negative mix signal for legacy Intel CPU-only HPC.
insights.locator: There is a stark contrast between what fell off

themes.theme: China and commercial exit from the list

insights.claim: China's TOP500 presence fell from 173 systems in November 2021 to just 18 now; China still holds #1 with LineShine but added only one new system this edition, CTyun HPC - shanghai15 using a MetaX C588 accelerator and China Telecom C86 CPUs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: China has largely stopped disclosing supercomputers publicly; Chinese domestic accelerators (MetaX) appear only sparsely, so the list understates Chinese compute.
insights.locator: China and Industry Submissions Have Collapsed

insights.claim: The TOP500 Industry segment has fallen from 258 systems in November 2021 to 146 now, and only 2 of the 28 new systems are Industry; the rest are 12 Research, 12 Academic and 2 Government.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Commercial AI/HPC buildouts are happening off-list, so TOP500 stats are a poor demand indicator.
insights.locator: The Industry segment has fallen

insights.claim: ServeTheHome's Patrick Kennedy argues the TOP500 is no longer a census of HPC or AI deployments because commercial systems have largely stopped appearing and current investment often prioritizes other benchmarks or deployment models.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Use vendor earnings and hyperscaler capex, not TOP500, to gauge AI infrastructure demand.
insights.quote: It feels like the Top500 submissions are not a census of all HPC or AI deployments
insights.locator: This is the same theme we raised

insights.claim: HPE led November 2026 TOP500 new systems with 8 entries and about 615 PF/s of new Rmax, dominated by KISTI's HANGANG (#12, 342.6 PF/s, HPE Cray EX254n with NVIDIA GH200 and Slingshot 400) and ORNL's Lux (#14, 220.79 PF/s, AMD EPYC 9575F with Instinct MI355X).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: HPE retains dominance in large public research supercomputers.
insights.locator: Who Built the New Systems

insights.claim: Behind HPE, Lenovo had 6 new TOP500 systems, MEGWARE 4, and Dell and Fujitsu 3 each, with all three Fujitsu entries built on Supermicro platforms, including RIKEN's RIKYU on GB200.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Supermicro is gaining indirect share in research HPC via OEM partnerships such as Fujitsu.
insights.quote: Notably, all three of Fujitsu’s entries are Supermicro-based platforms
insights.locator: Lenovo has 6 new systems

insights.claim: Europe led new TOP500 entries with 11 systems versus Asia's 9 and North America's 8, with Germany adding 6 new systems against the United States' 7.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: European sovereign HPC spending is visible in public lists while US commercial buildouts are not.
insights.locator: By geography, Europe leads

themes.theme: CPU shift: AMD, Grace, Intel decline

insights.claim: Among the 28 new TOP500 systems, AMD CPUs lead with 13 while NVIDIA Grace and Intel each have 7; all 5 new CPU-only systems are AMD-based (4 on Turin Dense Zen 5c), and all 7 new Intel systems are GPU hosts with no new Intel CPU-only systems.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Intel is losing HPC CPU sockets to AMD for CPU-only compute and to NVIDIA Grace for GPU hosts.
insights.locator: CPUs: Grace Ties Intel as AMD Leads x86

insights.claim: In the latest pre-Venice/Vera CPU generation on the TOP500, Intel has only one Granite Rapids system while AMD's Turin has 11.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A stark generational share gap that bears on Intel's data-center CPU competitiveness.
insights.quote: Intel has only one Granite Rapids CPU system, while AMD’s Turin has 11 systems
insights.locator: All seven new Intel systems are GPU hosts

insights.claim: Intel's share of all TOP500 systems has fallen to 50.2% from 82% in November 2021, while AMD sits at 39.8% and NVIDIA Grace powers 6.4% (32 systems).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Long-run share trend favors AMD and NVIDIA Arm CPUs over Intel in HPC.
insights.locator: Across the full list, Intel’s share

insights.claim: NVIDIA Grace is the most common CPU among new TOP500 systems with 7 appearances, all as GPU host, while on the full list the 2021-era AMD EPYC 7763 remains the most common SKU with 34 systems and Grace is close behind at 32.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's Arm CPU attach via superchips is steadily displacing x86 GPU hosts.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Grace is the most common CPU among new systems

insights.claim: New TOP500 CPU-only systems all use 96-192 core parts, while GPU-host CPUs typically have 36-72 cores; the median new system has 72 cores per socket versus 52 for the full list and 20 five years ago, and systems with 24 or fewer cores fell from 75% of the list in November 2021 to 19%.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Bifurcated CPU design: high-density EPYC for CPU compute, moderate-core hosts for GPUs, a mix favoring AMD and Arm.
insights.locator: Core Counts Split by Role

insights.claim: 14 of the 28 new TOP500 systems use NVIDIA Blackwell (12 B200, 2 GB200) and 6 use Hopper; Blackwell systems on the full list nearly doubled from 18 to 32 since June 2026, but Hopper with 137 systems remains the dominant installed base and 61 Ampere A100-era systems remain.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVIDIA dominates new accelerated HPC; the long Hopper/Ampere tail implies multi-year upgrade cycles.
insights.locator: Accelerators: NVIDIA Blackwell Arrives, but Hopper Is Still the Installed Base

insights.claim: Accelerated systems now represent 58.6% of TOP500 systems and 78.8% of Rmax versus 30% of systems in November 2021, while AMD Instinct across all generations is roughly at Blackwell's system count.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Accelerators now account for most HPC performance; AMD Instinct retains a meaningful public-HPC footprint.
insights.locator: Across the full list, accelerated systems

insights.claim: 19 of 28 new TOP500 systems use InfiniBand (14 NDR, 2 XDR, 2 HDR), 5 use HPE Slingshot including the first Slingshot 400 systems, and only 4 use Ethernet, including NVIDIA Spectrum-X at CINECA's MEGARIDE and HPE Juniper with AMD Pensando 400G at ORNL's Lux.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVIDIA InfiniBand retains HPC interconnect dominance; Ethernet AI fabrics remain rare among public HPC submissions.
insights.locator: Interconnect: InfiniBand Keeps Taking Share

insights.claim: Ethernet's share of all TOP500 systems has fallen from 45% in November 2021 to 18% as old 10/25/100GbE commercial clusters aged off, while InfiniBand rose to 60% (302 systems) and Slingshot is at 15% (73 systems).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The Ethernet decline reflects commercial clusters leaving the list rather than necessarily losing deployments, a composition effect to account for.
insights.locator: Across the full list, Ethernet has fallen

insights.claim: Half of new TOP500 systems run 400Gb/s per port and two run 800Gb/s XDR InfiniBand, nominal line rates that indicate where high-end cluster networking is heading.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: 800G networking is entering HPC deployments, supporting demand for next-gen NICs, switches and optics.
insights.locator: Half of the new systems run 400Gb/s per port
